Case report
A 63-year-old man presented with recurrent generalized epi-
leptic seizures for one day. Memory loss, behavioural chang-
es, and walking difficulties were also reported for the last 4
weeks. The patient had a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus
and melanoma, surgically removed 12 years ago. His melano-
ma recurred with lung involvement and was treated with
nivolumab for 3 months before neurological presentation.
On admission, neurological examination showed spatial
and temporal disorientation, mild persistent left hemiparesis,
lower extremity spasticity, hyperreflexia, and bilateral
Babinski signs, an ataxic syndrome with inability to walk,
asymmetric upper limb dysmetria, and bilateral horizontal

persistent nystagmus. Axial, proximal upper, and lower limb
stiffness with spasms and sensitivity to external stimuli
and hyperekplexia were also noted (modified Rankin
scale (mRS) = 5).
On brain MRI, limbic involvement was observed (Fig.1A, B)
in absence of spinal cord lesions. EEG showed bilateral asym-
metrical temporal slowing with dysregulated activity and isolated
sharp waves (Fig. 1C). On CSF analysis, mild pleocytosis (19
cells/μL) and CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands were observed in
absence of atypical cells. Extensive infectious screening yielded
negative results, and GAD65-IgG were detected in both serum
and CSF with Western blot (Eu roimmun, Luebeck) and con-
firmed on rat-brain immunofluorescence and with
radioimmunoprecipitation (80 nmol/L in serum, normal ≤
0.02). Whole-body CT excluded concomitant malignancies.
Nivolumab was discontinued, and treatment with intravenous
steroids (1 g/day for 5 days) associated after 1 week to intrave-
nous immunoglobulins (2 g/kg in 5 days) and lacosamide was
initiated followed by oral steroids tapered over the next months,
with a subsequent significant improvement. At discharge, the
patient was well-oriented and able to walk (mRS = 3).
Stiffness, dysmetria, and nystagmus significantly improved.
Three months later, repeat MRI and EEG showed a signif-
icant improvement (Fig. 1 D ,E ,F). The patient was able to
walk without assistance and bedside cognitive exam was
normal (mRS = 1). No recurrence of malignancy was noted
on whole-body PET-CT. However, 4 months later, epileptic
seizures recurred together with worsening of cerebellar symp-
toms; some improvement was noticed with intravenous im-
munoglobulins and levetiracetam (mRS = 2). Unfortunately,
the patient had cancer progression with lung and bone metas-
tases and subsequent worsening of epileptic seizures and cog-
nitive impairment 3 months after the last IVIG treatment. The
patient died 13 months after neurological symptoms onset.
Discussion
GAD65 antibodies can be associated with heterogeneous neuro-
logical syndromes, including stiff person syndrome/PERM, limbic
encephalitis, ataxia, and epilepsy; they are rarely paraneoplastic
[5]. In agreement with previous data on ICI-related adverse events,
these symptoms occurred early after therapy initiation in absence
of cancer recurrence and were responsive to immunosuppressive
therapy [3], thus supporting the role of nivolumab in reducing
immune tolerance and triggering autoimmune syndromes.
Among ICI-treated patients who develop neurological complica-
tions, GAD65-related disorders are extremely rare, and the 3 cases
previously described presented with isolated limbic encephalitis
responsive to immunosuppression [4, 6, 7].

The overlapping presentations of our case cover the full
spectrum of GAD65 autoimmunity, a presumed cytotoxic T
cell–mediated syndrome, and were triggered by the potentia-
tion of immune responses by the ICI. Even though a
paraneoplastic immune response (i.e. cancer antigen driven)
is possible though extremely rare with GAD65 antibodies, ICI
can also unmask pre-existing immune responses or trigger
novel ones (i.e. non-cancer antigen driven).
The recurrence of the symptoms after discontinuation
of immunosuppressive therapy suggests that some pa-
tients may need to be treated for longer, even if the
ICI was discontinued as the effects of these treatments
can still be evident months after their discontinuation.
The aggravation of our patient might also have been
due to the progression of the underlying malignancy.
Cancer recurrence can be seen after discontinuation
of ICI and rechallenge with the same or a different
ICI can be discussed on a case-to-case basis. In our
patient, given the severity of the immune-related ad-
verse events, even though the response to immunosup-
pressive therapy was positive, we avoided restarting ICI
and opted for palliative treatment as he also had pro-
gression of his oncological disease.
Conclusion
This case expands the spectrum of GAD65-associated condi-
tions induced by ICI. Even though the patient responded to
immunosuppressive therapy, which is often not seen in idio-
pathic GAD65 autoimmunity, cancer recurred after ICI dis-
continuation and the patient died. The complexity of these
cases requires a multidisciplinary approach with the oncolo-
gists, neurologists, and other specialists given the common
systemic complications.
